issues.legal_issue: A privately prepared map is not relevant or presumptively accurate unless the requirements for relying on published or official maps are established.
material_facts: The appellants relied on an undated wall map whose sources and accuracy were not established.
There was no satisfactory evidence that maps of that kind were generally offered for public sale.
The trial court rejected the map and gave reasons for finding it inaccurate; the appellants did not establish grounds to overturn those findings.
issues.conclusion: The map was irrelevant because its general public sale was not proved, and its accuracy could not be presumed or was otherwise unestablished.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 36 of the Evidence Act, statements in published maps are relevant when the maps are generally offered for public sale, while maps made under government authority may also qualify. Under section 83, the presumption of accuracy applies to maps or plans made under government authority, not to maps made for a case; a map outside that category must be proved accurate. The Court relied on the trial court’s supported findings about the map and the affidavit offered to establish public sale.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition.
predicates.privately_prepared_map_relied_on: A party relies on a privately prepared map to support its case.
predicates.public_sale_not_proved: The party relying on the map does not establish that maps of that kind were generally offered for public sale.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a dismissed writ petition relies on a privately prepared map without proof of general public sale, the map is not accepted as relevant evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The burden of proving that the proposed governmental action is unlawful does not shift merely because the location of villages is said to be within the government’s special knowledge.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the proposed transfer and argued that the locations of villages in different administrative areas were within the respondents’ special knowledge.
Both sides produced maps.
The trial court rejected the appellants’ maps as unreliable and accepted the respondents’ maps as credible.
The Court found that village locations were not within the respondents’ exclusive knowledge.
issues.conclusion: The burden did not shift to the respondents; the appellants bore the primary burden of establishing that the proposed action was unlawful, and no question of onus arose in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Evidence Act applies to facts especially within a party’s knowledge, but the location of villages was not within the respondents’ exclusive knowledge. Where both sides produce maps and the court assesses their reliability, the ordinary burden remains on the party alleging illegality to support that allegation.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and challenger_alleges_illegal_action and location_not_exclusively_known_to_respondent and both_sides_produce_maps

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition.
predicates.challenger_alleges_illegal_action: A party asks the court to restrain governmental action as unlawful.
predicates.location_not_exclusively_known_to_respon: The location in dispute is not a fact exclusively within the government respondent’s knowledge.
predicates.both_sides_produce_maps: Both the challenger and the government respondent produce maps bearing on the disputed location.

issues.definition: When a challenger alleges unlawful governmental action, the location is not exclusively known to the government, and both sides produce maps, the challenger retains the burden of proving illegality.

issues.legal_issue: A direction to divide a territory horizontally into northern and southern portions does not require a mathematically exact straight-line division when the governing text calls for an approximate equal division and supplies contextual guidance.
material_facts: The governing text required an area to be divided half and half, with the northern portion retained and the southern portion transferred.
It described the division as horizontal and as starting from a specified point, and also gave guidance concerning the treatment of enclaves.
The appellants argued that the text required a strict mathematical line and relied on a map that the trial court rejected as unreliable.
The Court found that the text indicated broadly where the division should begin and required an approximate division, rather than a geometrical construction.
issues.conclusion: The text did not require a strict mathematical line; it was capable of implementation by dividing the area approximately in half in accordance with the stated directional and contextual guidance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted the division provision as a whole: the requirement of a horizontal division indicated its general direction and starting point, while the half-and-half requirement and the related enclave provisions supplied practical guidance. The provision did not prescribe a mathematical line or exact geometrical halves.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition challenging implementation of a territorial division.
predicates.governing_text_requires_directional_half: The governing text calls for a territorial division in a stated direction, broadly from a stated starting point, and into two approximately equal parts.
predicates.challenger_relies_on_strict_line_interpr: The challenger contends that the stated direction requires a precise mathematical line.

issues.definition: When a territorial division is described directionally and calls for approximate halves, a strict-line objection does not prevent implementation merely because it assumes a mathematical division.

issues.legal_issue: A portion of territory previously allotted to another country may be transferred to that country when reliable evidence establishes that the portion belongs to an allotted area and was omitted from the earlier transfer.
material_facts: The respondents proposed to transfer a portion of a village to Pakistan.
The respondents’ maps, official jurisdiction material, and notification placed the village within the administrative area allotted to Pakistan under the Radcliffe Award.
The evidence supported the finding that there was one relevant village, rather than a separate village in the adjoining administrative area.
The portion at issue had not been delivered to Pakistan when the earlier partition was implemented.
Private documents relied on by the appellants did not identify the lands in a way that displaced the maps and official material.
issues.conclusion: The proposed transfer was a delivery of territory that had been allotted to Pakistan but inadvertently left undelivered, and the appellants established no valid objection to it on the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the maps, official jurisdiction material, and notification against the appellants’ private documents. It accepted the reliable material showing that the disputed portion formed part of the area allotted to Pakistan under the Radcliffe Award and had been omitted from the earlier delivery.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition challenging a proposed territorial transfer.
predicates.reliable_official_material_places_territ: Reliable maps or official records place the disputed territory within an area allotted to another country.
predicates.territory_omitted_from_prior_delivery: The disputed territory was not delivered to that country when the earlier allocation was implemented.

issues.definition: When reliable official material places territory within an allocation to another country and that territory was omitted from the earlier delivery, a later delivery is not unlawful merely because it occurs later.

issues.legal_issue: Territory administered as part of a province only because it was inadvertently left undelivered to another country does not become part of that province under a constitutional description covering territory administered as if it formed part of the province.
material_facts: A portion of territory had been allotted to Pakistan under the Radcliffe Award but was inadvertently not transferred at partition.
The territory was administered by the provincial government, which knew that it belonged to Pakistan and was to be transferred to it.
The territory had not become part of the province through a merger or a comparable arrangement.
The appellants argued that the administration of the territory brought it within the constitutional description of the province.
issues.conclusion: The territory did not become part of the province through its interim administration, so the proposed transfer did not require a further constitutional procedure on the basis asserted by the appellants.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 13 of the First Schedule to the Constitution, read in its historical context and alongside section 290A of the Government of India Act, 1935, covered territories administered as if they formed part of a province in circumstances associated with the merger of territories. The words “as if” did not cover territory administered with knowledge that it belonged to another country and had to be transferred to it. The Court also relied on article 1 and the earlier opinion in Special Reference No. 1 of 1959 concerning the constitutional procedure for ceding national territory; it held that the disputed territory had not become part of India or the province through accidental non-transfer.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and territory_administered_temporarily_as_provincial and administration_known_to_be_temporary and territory_not_added_by_merger

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition challenging a territorial transfer.
predicates.territory_administered_temporarily_as_pr: A government administers territory as part of a province for a time.
predicates.administration_known_to_be_temporary: The government knows that the territory belongs to another country and is to be transferred to it.
predicates.territory_not_added_by_merger: The territory did not become part of the province through a merger or comparable arrangement.

issues.definition: When territory is administered provisionally with knowledge that it belongs to another country, and it was not added to the province by merger, that administration does not make it part of the province.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that another country’s title was lost through adverse possession cannot be introduced for the first time on appeal when the governments involved do not claim adverse possession, and the court need not decide the claim’s merits.
material_facts: The appellants raised adverse possession only during the appeal and conceded that the plea had not been made in the writ petition.
The Union and the State respondents did not claim that their possession was adverse; they maintained that the territory belonged to Pakistan and should be delivered to it.
issues.conclusion: The adverse-possession contention was not entertained, and the Court found it unnecessary to decide whether such a claim could be made under international law or whether the evidence would support it.
issues.legal_principle: A contention not raised in the original writ petition could not be introduced in the appeal in the circumstances of this case, particularly where the governmental parties whose possession was invoked expressly disclaimed any claim of adverse possession. The Court therefore did not reach the international-law or evidentiary merits.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_first_raised_on: A party first raises an adverse-possession claim during the appeal, not in the original petition.
predicates.government_parties_disclaim_adverse_clai: The government parties whose possession is relied on do not assert that their possession was adverse.

issues.definition: When an adverse-possession claim is raised only on appeal and the government parties disclaim such a claim, the court does not entertain it on appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Union territories are included in the meaning of “State” for interpreting the constitutional provision on changes to state territories, but correcting that point does not displace the conclusion that ceding national territory requires constitutional amendment.
material_facts: In an earlier constitutional reference, the Court had assumed that the word “State” in the relevant constitutional provision excluded Union territories.
The Court identified section 3(58)(b) of the General Clauses Act and article 367(1) as requiring that the word include Union territories unless the context otherwise requires.

The earlier conclusion about the constitutional procedure for ceding territory rested primarily on the sovereign character of the power to cede or acquire territory, not on the assumption about Union territories.
The constitutional amendment at issue had been passed in the manner indicated in the earlier reference.
issues.conclusion: The earlier assumption that Union territories were excluded was incorrect, but the conclusion that ceding national territory requires action under the constitutional amendment procedure remained unaffected.
issues.legal_principle: Article 367(1) applies the General Clauses Act, 1897, to interpretation of the Constitution unless the context otherwise requires. Section 3(58)(b) defines “State” to include a Union territory. The Court corrected its earlier contrary assumption in Special Reference No. 1 of 1959 but maintained that the power to cede national territory is an attribute of sovereignty and that a law under article 3 alone is insufficient; appropriate action under article 368 is required.

predicates.constitutional_reference_interprets_terr: The proceeding concerns interpretation of the constitutional power to alter or cede territory.
predicates.general_definition_includes_union_territ: The generally applicable interpretive definition of “State” includes Union territories unless the context requires otherwise.
predicates.cession_conclusion_based_on_sovereignty: The conclusion about the procedure for ceding national territory rests primarily on the sovereign character of that power.

issues.definition: When the interpretive definition includes Union territories but the cession procedure rests on the sovereign character of the power, Union territories are included without changing the requirement for constitutional amendment to cede territory.
